extraction.name: Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
extraction.description: A paper that systematically evaluates object hallucination in large vision-language models (LVLMs), analyzes how visual instruction data influences hallucination, and proposes POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) as a more stable and flexible evaluation method.
extraction.creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The paper evaluates object hallucination using MSCOCO validation images and human-labeled captions/annotations, and also constructs polling questions from ground-truth objects or automatically segmented objects using SEEM.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: The paper notes that POPE can be extended to unannotated datasets using automatic segmentation, and that some datasets lack annotations; it also mentions that results may differ when automatic segmentation labels are inconsistent with collected human annotations.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: MSCOCO validation set images with object annotations and human-labeled captions; additionally, images from A-OKVQA and GQA are segmented with SEEM for POPE construction.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For POPE, ground-truth objects are used to create 'Yes' questions and negative objects are sampled to create 'No' questions under random, popular, and adversarial sampling strategies; objects are also ranked by appearance or co-occurrence frequency for analysis.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: The authors randomly sampled 2,000 MSCOCO validation images for CHAIR evaluation and 500 MSCOCO validation images with more than 3 ground-truth objects for POPE; CHAIR evaluation follows prior settings considering only 80 MSCOCO objects.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human annotations provide ground-truth objects and captions in MSCOCO. For POPE, questions are formed from ground-truth objects or automatically segmented objects, and answers are binary ('Yes'/'No').
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The paper analyzes hallucination frequency by object appearance and co-occurrence, and reports that POPE responses are consistent with generated captions; it also discusses that automatic segmentation labels may diverge from human annotations.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For POPE, 6 questions per image were constructed in the MSCOCO evaluation setting.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) was used for automatic segmentation-based annotation.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The paper states that hallucination can degrade model performance and harm user experiences in real-world applications, and gives safety-related examples such as autonomous driving decisions being affected by incorrect understanding of the environment.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper argues that visual instruction datasets are unbalanced and that top frequent objects and frequently co-occurring objects are more likely to be hallucinated by LVLMs.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The study focuses only on object hallucination and does not measure overall LVLM performance; evaluation is limited to a part of each validation set due to computation constraints; POPE may be affected when models do not explicitly answer 'Yes' or 'No'; automatic segmentation labels may be inconsistent with human annotations; only a small number of LVLMs are evaluated.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Evaluation of object hallucination in LVLMs; benchmarking with CHAIR and POPE; comparison with VQA and image captioning performance.
